title: The crowd
hookLine: Seneca says he comes back from the games more cruel for having been among people

lines: A GOOD MOOD AT THE GAME.
cards: A fan arrives at the game in a good mood. By the third quarter he's on his feet, yelling things at a referee he'd be embarrassed to hear played back.
Someone opens the comments under a news story, just to see, and twenty minutes later comes away a little meaner. Nobody decided to get harsher. The crowd did it, a little at a time.
Seneca's seventh letter begins with a day like that, at the Roman arena.

teach.b: Lucilius asks what he should most avoid. Seneca answers: the crowd. Not people, but the mass of people pulling the same way.
You can't trust yourself to it yet, he says.

Then he confesses. He went to the midday show at the games hoping for something light, a little wit, a break. Instead he found plain killing, men sent out with no armor, and a crowd shouting for more.

Seneca gives the details, and they're grim. What matters is what he says next. He comes home more greedy, more ambitious, more given to pleasure, and more cruel and inhuman, because he has been among people.
One person's bad example does real harm, he says; a neighbor's greed or luxury rubs off. Shouted by thousands, it's stronger still.

Even Socrates, Cato or Laelius could have been shaken by a crowd like that. The cure: withdraw into yourself as much as you can, and spend time with people who will make you better, and people you can make better.
It works both ways: people learn while they teach.
Look back at this week: choose, then trust; face it; no costume; chained together; Hecaton; the living voice; and now, what I bring home. All seven ask one thing. Who are you letting shape you?

how: Following Seneca's seventh letter, some people pay attention to how crowds, in person or online, change their mood, and choose company that leaves them better.

o: the audience Seneca hoped to win with his letters
the mass of people whose habits rub off on you
the gladiators who fought at the Roman games

s: Seneca went to the games expecting cruelty
he hoped for something light and witty, and found plain killing.
Seneca says even Socrates could be shaken by a crowd
he names Socrates, Cato and Laelius.
Seneca says to avoid all people
he says to spend time with those who make you better, and those you can help.

games.q: you're Seneca. it's a holiday, and you go to the midday games hoping for a light show. what do you find?
o: plain killing, and a crowd shouting for more.
games.why: he found cruelty, not wit, and says he came home more cruel and inhuman for having been among people.

practice: Think back over the last few days to one crowd you spent time in, in person or on a screen: a feed, a group chat, a break room, a stadium. Ask honestly, without blame, what you brought home from it.
Maybe laughter and energy; maybe something a little harder, or more anxious.

wordCard.voice: The crowd. Seneca's seventh letter: the mass of people shapes us more than we notice, and we carry home what we picked up there. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: more inhuman, because I have been among human beings, Seneca's line in letter seven.

carryVoice: Your line: what I bring home. The company you keep comes home with you. A week of letters, done.
